::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain how a tree is grown by **recursive binary splitting**, and compute **Gini impurity** and **entropy** by hand for one split;
- grow a **regression tree** split and explain what it minimises;
- control tree size with **cost-complexity pruning** and apply the **1-SE rule** correctly;
- fit, plot and read a tree with `rpart` and `rpart.plot`, and tune it with `decision_tree()` in tidymodels;
- show that trees are **unstable** and explain why this motivates ensembles.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart)        # engine for decision trees
library(rpart.plot)   # tree plots

# tidymodels attaches modeldata, whose own `penguins` (with different column
# names) would mask the base-R one: make sure we use R's built-in version.
penguins <- datasets::penguins
```
:::


## 1. Why trees? The "20 questions" game

In the game *20 questions*, one player thinks of an object and the other must guess it by asking yes/no questions. Good players ask questions that **split the remaining possibilities as cleanly as possible**: "Is it alive?" is better than "Is it a toaster?".

A **decision tree** predicts in the same way. To predict whether a Titanic passenger survived it might ask: *Is the passenger male?* If yes: *Is he older than 9.5?* … Each question splits the passengers into two groups; at the end of each path (a **leaf**) the tree predicts the majority class (or the class proportions) of the training passengers who ended there.

Trees are attractive because they:

- are **easy to explain** — a tree with five leaves is a set of five rules;
- capture **non-linear effects and interactions** automatically (the effect of age can be different for men and women);
- need **no scaling** of predictors and handle categorical variables naturally.

Their weakness, as we will see, is **instability**: small changes in the data can produce a very different tree.

We use the same Titanic preparation as in [the ML workflow lesson](44-ml-workflow.qmd):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
titanic <- readr::read_csv(data_path("titanic_data.csv"),
                           na = c("", "NA", "?"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(survived, pclass, sex, age, sibsp, parch, fare, embarked) |>
  mutate(
    survived = factor(survived, levels = c(1, 0), labels = c("yes", "no")),
    pclass   = factor(pclass, levels = 1:3, labels = c("1st", "2nd", "3rd")),
    sex      = factor(sex),
    embarked = factor(embarked)
  )

set.seed(2026)
titanic_split <- initial_split(titanic, prop = 0.75, strata = survived)
titanic_train <- training(titanic_split)
titanic_test  <- testing(titanic_split)
set.seed(2026)
titanic_folds <- vfold_cv(titanic_train, v = 5, strata = survived)
titanic_metrics <- metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity,
                              brier_class, mn_log_loss)
```
:::


## 2. How a classification tree chooses a split

### Impurity

A group of passengers is **pure** if they all share the same fate. We need a number that is 0 for a pure group and large for a mixed one. With class proportions $p_1, \dots, p_K$ in a node, the two common choices are

$$
\text{Gini} = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2, \qquad \text{Entropy} = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k .
$$

For two classes, both are 0 when $p = 0$ or $p = 1$ and largest at $p = 0.5$ (Gini 0.5, entropy 1).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
gini <- function(counts) {
  p <- counts / sum(counts)
  1 - sum(p^2)
}
entropy <- function(counts) {
  p <- counts / sum(counts)
  p <- p[p > 0]                # 0 * log(0) is taken as 0
  -sum(p * log2(p))
}
```
:::


### One split by hand: sex


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tab <- table(titanic$sex, titanic$survived)
tab
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>         
#>          yes  no
#>   female 339 127
#>   male   161 682
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
root <- colSums(tab)                     # all passengers together
w <- rowSums(tab) / sum(tab)             # share of passengers in each child
gini_children <- apply(tab, 1, gini)
entropy_children <- apply(tab, 1, entropy)

c(gini_root = gini(root),
  gini_after = sum(w * gini_children),
  entropy_root = entropy(root),
  entropy_after = sum(w * entropy_children))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     gini_root    gini_after  entropy_root entropy_after 
#>        0.4721        0.3402        0.9594        0.7539
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- Before splitting, the Gini impurity of all passengers is 0.472.
- After splitting by sex, each child is purer: Gini 0.397 for women and 0.309 for men. Their **weighted average** (weights = share of passengers) is 0.34.
- The **decrease in impurity** is 0.132 (Gini) or 0.206 bits (entropy; this decrease is called the *information gain*).
:::

The tree-growing algorithm simply tries **every possible split of every predictor** — for a numeric variable, every threshold between consecutive values; for a factor, groupings of its levels — and picks the one with the largest decrease in impurity. Let us check that "sex" beats "3rd class vs the rest":


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tab_cl <- table(titanic$pclass == "3rd", titanic$survived)
w_cl <- rowSums(tab_cl) / sum(tab_cl)
c(sex = gini(root) - sum(w * gini_children),
  third_class = gini(root) - sum(w_cl * apply(tab_cl, 1, gini)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>         sex third_class 
#>     0.13197     0.03793
```


:::
:::


Then the same search is repeated **inside each child**, and again inside the grandchildren: this is **recursive binary splitting**. It is *greedy*: each split is the best one at that moment, without looking ahead.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: why not just use the error rate?

One could measure impurity with the misclassification rate $1 - \max_k p_k$. It is rarely used for growing trees because it is not sensitive enough: many splits produce the same error rate even though one of them creates a much purer child. Gini and entropy are strictly concave in $p$, so any split that changes the class proportions strictly reduces them. In practice Gini and entropy almost always choose the same splits; `rpart` uses Gini by default (`parms = list(split = "information")` switches to entropy).
:::

## 3. Regression trees

For a numeric outcome, a leaf predicts the **mean** of its training observations, and impurity is the **sum of squared errors** (SSE) around that mean. A split at threshold $s$ on predictor $x$ is chosen to minimise

$$
\sum_{i:\,x_i < s} (y_i - \bar y_{\text{left}})^2 + \sum_{i:\,x_i \ge s} (y_i - \bar y_{\text{right}})^2 .
$$

Let us find the best single split of penguin body mass on flipper length:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
peng <- penguins[!is.na(penguins$body_mass) & !is.na(penguins$flipper_len), ]

best_split <- function(x, y) {
  cuts <- sort(unique(x))
  cuts <- (head(cuts, -1) + tail(cuts, -1)) / 2   # midpoints
  sse <- vapply(cuts, \(s) {
    left <- y[x < s]
    right <- y[x >= s]
    sum((left - mean(left))^2) + sum((right - mean(right))^2)
  }, numeric(1))
  list(cut = cuts[which.min(sse)], cuts = cuts, sse = sse)
}
sp <- best_split(peng$flipper_len, peng$body_mass)
sp$cut
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 206.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
tapply(peng$body_mass, peng$flipper_len < sp$cut, mean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>  5032  3699
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(sp$cuts, sp$sse / 1e6, type = "l",
     xlab = "Threshold on flipper length (mm)", ylab = "SSE (millions)")
abline(v = sp$cut, lty = 2)
plot(peng$flipper_len, peng$body_mass, col = "grey50",
     xlab = "Flipper length (mm)", ylab = "Body mass (g)")
means <- tapply(peng$body_mass, peng$flipper_len >= sp$cut, mean)
segments(c(min(peng$flipper_len), sp$cut), means,
         c(sp$cut, max(peng$flipper_len)), means, lwd = 3, col = "#D55E00")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Left: SSE of every candidate split; the minimum gives the best threshold. Right: the resulting one-split regression tree (a step function).](45-decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-reg-split-1.png){#fig-reg-split fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


The best split, at 206.5 mm, reduces the SSE by 65% compared with predicting the overall mean. A full regression tree repeats this inside each half, producing a step function with more and more steps.

## 4. Growing and pruning a tree with `rpart`

### A deliberately large tree


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
tree_full <- rpart(
  survived ~ ., data = titanic_train, method = "class",
  control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 10, xval = 10)
)
nrow(tree_full$frame[tree_full$frame$var == "<leaf>", ])   # number of leaves
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 50
```


:::
:::


With `cp = 0` and `minsplit = 10`, the tree keeps splitting as long as a node has at least 10 passengers: it grows 50 leaves and certainly overfits. (`rpart` handles the missing ages itself, using *surrogate* splits on correlated variables.)

### Cost-complexity pruning

Instead of stopping early, the standard strategy is to grow a large tree and then **prune** it back. For a value $\alpha \ge 0$, pruning finds the subtree $T$ that minimises

$$
R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\, |T|,
$$

where $R(T)$ is the training error and $|T|$ the number of leaves. $\alpha = 0$ keeps the full tree; a large $\alpha$ prunes everything back to the root. `rpart` calls a rescaled version of $\alpha$ the **complexity parameter** `cp`, and for every candidate `cp` it reports a 10-fold cross-validated error:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
printcp(tree_full)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> Classification tree:
#> rpart(formula = survived ~ ., data = titanic_train, method = "class", 
#>     control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 10, xval = 10))
#> 
#> Variables actually used in tree construction:
#> [1] age      embarked fare     parch    pclass   sex      sibsp   
#> 
#> Root node error: 375/981 = 0.38
#> 
#> n= 981 
#> 
#>         CP nsplit rel error xerror  xstd
#> 1  0.42400      0      1.00   1.00 0.041
#> 2  0.02267      1      0.58   0.58 0.035
#> 3  0.02133      3      0.53   0.55 0.034
#> 4  0.01422      5      0.49   0.53 0.033
#> 5  0.00800      8      0.45   0.51 0.033
#> 6  0.00533     10      0.43   0.52 0.033
#> 7  0.00400     12      0.42   0.54 0.034
#> 8  0.00311     23      0.37   0.52 0.033
#> 9  0.00267     29      0.35   0.53 0.034
#> 10 0.00178     35      0.33   0.53 0.034
#> 11 0.00133     38      0.33   0.53 0.034
#> 12 0.00089     42      0.32   0.56 0.034
#> 13 0.00067     45      0.32   0.57 0.034
#> 14 0.00000     49      0.32   0.57 0.034
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- Each row is a subtree. `CP` is the complexity parameter at which it becomes optimal, `nsplit` its number of splits (leaves = `nsplit + 1`).
- `rel error` is the **training** error relative to the root (it always decreases).
- `xerror` is the **cross-validated** error relative to the root, and `xstd` its standard error. These are the columns to use for choosing the size.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plotcp(tree_full)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-validated relative error versus cp (and tree size). The horizontal line is drawn one standard error above the minimum.](45-decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-plotcp-1.png){#fig-plotcp fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


### The 1-SE rule — done correctly

Picking the row with the smallest `xerror` tends to select trees that are larger than necessary: the CV curve is often flat near its minimum, and the exact minimum is partly noise. The **one-standard-error rule** (Breiman et al., 1984) chooses **the simplest tree whose CV error is within one standard error of the minimum**:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
cpt <- tree_full$cptable
i_min <- which.min(cpt[, "xerror"])                       # minimum CV error
threshold <- cpt[i_min, "xerror"] + cpt[i_min, "xstd"]   # min + 1 SE
i_1se <- which(cpt[, "xerror"] <= threshold)[1]           # simplest such tree
c(splits_min = cpt[i_min, "nsplit"], splits_1se = cpt[i_1se, "nsplit"])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> splits_min splits_1se 
#>          8          5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
tree_1se <- prune(tree_full, cp = cpt[i_1se, "CP"])
```
:::


Rows of `cptable` are ordered from the simplest tree (largest `cp`) to the most complex, so the **first** row under the threshold is the simplest acceptable tree. (The old version of this lesson announced the 1-SE rule but took `which.min(xerror)`, i.e. the minimum — a different rule.) Here the minimum-error tree has 8 splits and the 1-SE tree 5.

### Reading the pruned tree


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rpart.plot(tree_1se, extra = 104, under = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The pruned tree (1-SE rule). Each box shows the predicted class, the predicted probability of each class (yes, no), and the percentage of training passengers in the node.](45-decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-tree-1se-1.png){#fig-tree-1se fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


Read a path from the root to a leaf as a rule. The first split is on `sex`, as our hand calculation suggested. The same rules in text form:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rpart.rules(tree_1se, cover = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>  survived                                                                                    cover
#>      0.07 when sex is female & pclass is 1st or 2nd                                            19%
#>      0.10 when sex is   male                        & age <  9.5              & sibsp <  3      2%
#>      0.45 when sex is female & pclass is        3rd              & fare <  25                  15%
#>      0.83 when sex is   male                        & age >= 9.5                               61%
#>      0.92 when sex is   male                        & age <  9.5              & sibsp >= 3      1%
#>      0.94 when sex is female & pclass is        3rd              & fare >= 25                   2%
```


:::
:::


For a two-class outcome, `rpart.rules()` prints the fitted probability of the **second** level of the outcome (here `no`, i.e. death) — check the column header it prints. `cover` is the percentage of training passengers following each rule.

## 5. Tuning a tree with tidymodels

The `rpart` CV is convenient but specific to rpart. In tidymodels we tune the tree like any other model, with the same folds and metrics as the logistic regression of lesson 44, so the results are directly comparable.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tree_spec <- decision_tree(cost_complexity = tune(), tree_depth = tune(),
                           min_n = 10) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("classification")

tree_rec <- recipe(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors())

tree_wf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  add_model(tree_spec)
```
:::


Trees need neither dummy variables nor normalisation, so the recipe only imputes missing values (rpart could also handle them on its own; imputing keeps the pipeline identical across models).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(),
                          tree_depth(range = c(1L, 10L)),
                          levels = c(5, 4))
nrow(tree_grid)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 20
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
tree_res <- tune_grid(tree_wf, resamples = titanic_folds,
                      grid = tree_grid, metrics = titanic_metrics)
```
:::


A grid of 20 combinations × 5 folds = 100 fits; trees are fast, so this takes seconds.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
autoplot(tree_res, metric = c("roc_auc", "brier_class"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cross-validated performance of trees by cost-complexity and maximum depth.](45-decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-tune-tree-1.png){#fig-tune-tree fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
show_best(tree_res, metric = "roc_auc", n = 5)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   cost_complexity tree_depth .metric .estimator   mean     n std_err .config    
#>             <dbl>      <int> <chr>   <chr>       <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>      
#> 1   0.0000000001           7 roc_auc binary     0.8463     5 0.01823 pre0_mod03…
#> 2   0.00000001778          7 roc_auc binary     0.8463     5 0.01823 pre0_mod07…
#> 3   0.000003162            7 roc_auc binary     0.8463     5 0.01823 pre0_mod11…
#> 4   0.0005623              7 roc_auc binary     0.8463     5 0.01823 pre0_mod15…
#> 5   0.0000000001          10 roc_auc binary     0.8326     5 0.01600 pre0_mod04…
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
best_tree <- select_by_one_std_err(tree_res, desc(cost_complexity),
                                   tree_depth, metric = "roc_auc")
best_tree
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>   cost_complexity tree_depth .config         
#>             <dbl>      <int> <chr>           
#> 1       0.0005623          7 pre0_mod15_post0
```

`select_best()` would return the combination with the highest mean AUC. `select_by_one_std_err()` implements the 1-SE rule: among combinations within one standard error of the best, it returns the **simplest**, where we define "simple" by sorting on `desc(cost_complexity)` (more pruning) and then `tree_depth` (shallower).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

  finalize_workflow(best_tree) |>
  last_fit(titanic_split, metrics = titanic_metrics)
collect_metrics(tree_final)

## 6. Trees are unstable

Fit the same kind of tree on four **bootstrap samples** of the training data (samples of the same size, drawn with replacement — see [the bootstrap lesson](../07-probability/31-bootstrap.qmd)):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(45)
boot_trees <- lapply(1:4, \(b) {
  idx <- sample(nrow(titanic_train), replace = TRUE)
  rpart(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train[idx, ], method = "class",
        control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01))
})
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (tr in boot_trees) rpart.plot(tr, extra = 0, cex = 0.7)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Four trees fitted to four bootstrap samples of the same training data.](45-decision-trees_files/figure-html/fig-boot-trees-1.png){#fig-boot-trees fig-align='center' width=85%}
:::
:::


The first split (sex) is stable, because its signal is strong. Below it, the trees choose different variables and thresholds. Predictions for a single passenger can change a lot:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
passenger <- tibble(
  pclass = factor("2nd", levels = levels(titanic$pclass)),
  sex = factor("male", levels = levels(titanic$sex)),
  age = 30, sibsp = 0, parch = 0, fare = 13,
  embarked = factor("S", levels = levels(titanic$embarked))
)
set.seed(45)
p_boot <- replicate(50, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(titanic_train), replace = TRUE)
  fit <- rpart(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train[idx, ], method = "class",
               control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01))
  predict(fit, passenger, type = "prob")[, "yes"]
})
summary(p_boot)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.0937  0.1346  0.1593  0.1534  0.1729  0.1969
```


:::
:::


Across 50 bootstrap trees, the predicted survival probability of a 30-year-old man in 2nd class ranges from 0.09 to 0.2. This is the **high variance** of section 3 of lesson 44, in action. Because each split depends on the previous ones, a small change near the top propagates down the whole tree.

The natural cure is to **average many trees**: averaging reduces variance. This is the idea behind [random forests](46-random-forests.qmd) and, in a different way, [boosting](47-gradient-boosting.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Keeping the unpruned tree.** A tree grown until leaves are pure has near-zero training error and poor test performance. Prune (or tune `cost_complexity` / `tree_depth` / `min_n`).
2. **Calling the minimum-xerror tree "the 1-SE tree".** The 1-SE rule picks the *simplest* tree within one SE of the minimum.
3. **Over-interpreting the structure.** A different sample could give a different tree; interpret only the strong, stable splits.
4. **Reading `printcp()`'s `rel error` as test error.** It is training error; use `xerror`.
5. **Forgetting `set.seed()`** before `rpart()`: its internal cross-validation is random, so `xerror` changes from run to run.
:::

## 7. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. A node contains 40 survivors and 60 non-survivors. What are its Gini impurity and entropy?

Gini $= 1 - (0.4^2 + 0.6^2) = 0.48$. Entropy $= -(0.4\log_2 0.4 + 0.6\log_2 0.6) \approx 0.971$ bits.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Why does `rel error` in `printcp()` always decrease, while `xerror` does not?

`rel error` is measured on the training data, and a larger tree can always fit the training data at least as well. `xerror` is measured on held-out folds, so beyond some size extra splits fit noise and the error stops falling or rises.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. Does a decision tree need standardised predictors?

No. A split "age < 9.5" is equivalent to "age in months < 114": any monotone transformation of a predictor gives the same partitions. Trees are invariant to scaling.
:::

[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — impurity by hand.** Using `gini()` and `entropy()`, compute the impurity decrease of the split "1st class vs the rest" on `titanic`. Is it better or worse than the split on sex?

## Solution
```r
tab_1st <- table(titanic$pclass == "1st", titanic$survived)
w_1st <- rowSums(tab_1st) / sum(tab_1st)
gini(root) - sum(w_1st * apply(tab_1st, 1, gini))
entropy(root) - sum(w_1st * apply(tab_1st, 1, entropy))
```
The decrease (about 0.04 for Gini) is much smaller than for sex (about 0.13): sex is the better first question.

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug the 1-SE rule.** A student writes `cp_1se <- cpt[which.min(cpt[, "xerror"] + cpt[, "xstd"]), "CP"]`. Explain what this selects, and why it is not the 1-SE rule.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
It picks the tree with the smallest value of `xerror + xstd` — a penalised minimum, which is usually the same tree as (or close to) the minimum-error tree. The 1-SE rule instead computes **one threshold** (the minimum `xerror` plus *its* `xstd`) and then takes the **simplest** tree (first row) whose `xerror` is below that threshold:
```r
i_min <- which.min(cpt[, "xerror"])
i_1se <- which(cpt[, "xerror"] <= cpt[i_min, "xerror"] + cpt[i_min, "xstd"])[1]
```
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
peng_tree <- rpart(body_mass ~ ., method = "anova",
                   data = select(penguins, -year))
rpart.plot(peng_tree)
```
Because the tree can now choose among all predictors (including `species` and `sex`), the first split need not be on flipper length: the algorithm takes the single split with the largest SSE reduction across all variables. Compare the root split in the plot with the threshold 206.5 mm found above. Leaves show the mean body mass (in grams) and the percentage of penguins.

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — quantify instability.** Repeat the bootstrap experiment of section 6 with 100 trees. For each tree record the **set of variables it uses** (hint: `tr$frame$var` lists the split variable of every node, and `"<leaf>"` for leaves). Tabulate the results: how many different variable sets appear?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
set.seed(45)
var_sets <- replicate(100, {
  idx <- sample(nrow(titanic_train), replace = TRUE)
  tr <- rpart(survived ~ ., data = titanic_train[idx, ], method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0.01))
  used <- setdiff(as.character(tr$frame$var), "<leaf>")
  paste(sort(unique(used)), collapse = ", ")
})
sort(table(var_sets), decreasing = TRUE)
length(unique(var_sets))
```
`sex` appears in every tree, but the other variables used (`age`, `pclass`, `fare`, `sibsp`, …) change from one bootstrap sample to the next, giving many distinct variable sets. Trees that look equally good on the data can tell different stories.
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| Gini $1-\sum p_k^2$, entropy $-\sum p_k\log_2 p_k$ | Impurity of a node (classification) |
| SSE around the mean | Impurity of a node (regression) |
| `rpart(y ~ ., method = "class")` | Grow a tree (`"anova"` for regression) |
| `printcp()`, `plotcp()`, `prune()` | Cost-complexity path and pruning |
| 1-SE rule | Simplest tree within 1 SE of the minimum CV error |
| `rpart.plot()`, `rpart.rules()` | Plot / list the rules |
| `decision_tree(cost_complexity, tree_depth, min_n)` | tidymodels specification (`set_engine("rpart")`) |
| `select_by_one_std_err()` | 1-SE rule for any tuning result |

- Trees split the data greedily with the question that most reduces impurity.
- Big trees overfit; **pruning** trades a little bias for much less variance.
- Trees are easy to read but **unstable** — small data changes, different trees.
- Averaging many trees fixes the instability: next lesson.
